newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil launches campaign to stamp out sex tourism.
newsitem.headline: Brazil launches campaign to stamp out sex tourism.

text.p: The Brazilian government on Wednesday launched a crackdown on sex tourism, warning foreigners who take advantage of widespread child prostitution that they will be jailed if caught.

Announcing a $400,000 publicity campaign among tour operators and in Brazil's top tourist destinations, Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles said the aim was to replace sex tourists with "eco-tourists."
"A country with our cultural heritage cannot allow its children to be exploited criminally," the minister, whose portfolio includes tourism, said at a ceremony.
"Foreigners who are caught will go to jail," Caio Luiz Carvalho, head of the federal Brazilian tourism agency Embratur, added in remarks to reporters.
Child welfare groups warn that Brazil is fast becoming an alternative for tourists seeking cheap and easy sex after a crackdown in traditional Southeast Asian destinations.
The impoverished northeast, its golden beaches and tropical climate creating a sultry sensuality, has become a destination of choice, especially for Europeans.
But child prostitution is not fed by tourism alone. Non-governmental organisations estimate that from 500,000 to two million Brazilian children live a life of vice in the country's main cities.
As part of the new campaign against abuse of children by tourists, the Brazilian government will help non-governmental organisations set up a free central telephone number to receive complaints.
Posters and stickers reminding tourists: "Careful -- Brazil is watching," will also be distributed in airplanes, taxis, hotels and travel agencies.

The Brazilian campaign comes some six months after an international conference in Stockholm on child sexual abuse at which Brazil and others called on the world community to help stamp out sex tourism.

Dornelles said "Ecotourism" was now the most sought after tourism service in the world and Brazil aimed to exploit the giant Amazon rain forest and the world's largest wetlands, the Pantanal, for all their worth.

"The year 1997 will be the year of tourism for Brazil," Dornelles said. "But in order for us to be proud of this activity, we must extinguish in a radical manner the sexual exploitation of children by tourists."
